finding: "`blocking` governs `clean` and nothing else" is falsified by the two sinks that consume `clean`, and the spec never says which behaviour is wanted. `next_action` is derived FROM `clean` at both audit outputs: internal/cli/audit_record.go:125 calls engine.AuditNextAction(specPath, converged, !clean) and audit_record.go:390 computes latestHasFindings := len(rounds) > 0 && !rounds[len(rounds)-1].Clean. Each site carries a comment asserting the equivalence this release breaks — "the just-recorded round is the latest, so its non-PASS rows are exactly !clean" and "the latest recorded round holding open non-PASS rows is exactly !Clean". Under `blocking`, the first clean round of a streak that still holds `warning`/`info` rows flips next_action from branch 2 ("address the findings, then re-audit") to branch 3 ("run the next audit round") with nothing anywhere naming the rows that were accepted — the same invisibility §4 exists to fix, on the one command §4 says the breakdown is NOT on. I have to invent this behaviour: §2 enumerates three surfaces that stay severity-blind (role_streaks[].open, consecutive_clean, spec_coverage_clean_rounds) and next_action is in neither that list nor the governed one.
suggestion: Add next_action to one of §2's two lists and say which branch a clean-with-open-rows round takes. Either it stays severity-blind (pass the non-PASS count, not !clean, so branch 2 still fires and the operator is still told rows are open), or it follows `clean` (branch 3) and §4's breakdown has to reach --record too, which Non-Goal 4 currently forbids. Also note in §6 that the two invariant comments at audit_record.go:124 and :389 stop being true, so the implementer does not leave them behind as the release's third and fourth false shipped claims.

finding: The `all` row of §2's table reads "no non-`PASS` row in the round carries any severity". Read either way that sentence makes a non-PASS row that carries NO severity harmless under `all`, so a round holding only such rows would be stamped clean. That is not the behaviour tp ships: internal/cli/audit_record.go:71 is `clean := findings == 0`, counted at line 248 through engine.AuditRowIsPass, which is byte-exact on `status` and never reads `severity` at all. So the default the release calls behaviour-preserving (§1 deliverable 1: "the behaviour tp ships today, so a project that does not set it sees no change") changes on install for every project whose auditors omit `severity` — and §7 test 8 puts `null` and absent severities in scope by its own construction. I cannot write task acceptance for the `all` half of the predicate from this text: the sentence and §1 give opposite answers and only the tree breaks the tie.
suggestion: Phrase the `all` row over existence rather than over severity: "no non-`PASS` row exists in the round" — which is `findings == 0` and is exactly what ships. Keep severity out of the `all` row entirely; it is only the `blocking` row that needs to grade. The paragraph below the table already explains why the population is the non-PASS rows, so nothing else needs to change.

finding: The record-time stamping decision is argued in one direction only, and the unargued direction is the fail-open one. §2 justifies stamping by what a live recompute would do to history when the knob is SET (67 out-of-enum legacy rows would be re-graded blocking and converged cycles would report `converged: false`) — a strict-making direction. It never says what happens when the knob is UNSET or moved back to `all`. Under stamping the answer is that nothing happens: a round recorded under `blocking` keeps `clean: true` for ever, and the audit path's convergence reads the stored flag (`ConsecutiveClean(st.AuditRounds)` / `Converged(st.AuditRounds, …)` over the stored `Clean`), so a cycle can later converge under `all` on rounds that were only ever clean under `blocking`, with the `error`-free-but-not-finding-free rows still open. One human-approved round of `blocking` therefore relaxes that cycle's convergence permanently and irreversibly without a re-record. This is precisely the relaxation §3's fence exists to prevent a unit from obtaining, obtained instead by an operator who later changes their mind and cannot take it back. §7 test 9 pins only the safe direction (record under `all`, switch to `blocking`).
suggestion: Say normatively what a switch back to `all` (or an unset) does to rounds already stamped under `blocking`: either those rounds' verdicts are re-graded on the next `--record` (and then explain why the 67-legacy-row argument does not also apply), or they are permanently accepted (and then say so as a deliberate consequence, and add the missing half to test 9: record under `blocking`, switch to `all`, assert the stored verdicts and `converged`).

finding: The table's `all` row is severity-quantified and therefore is NOT the behaviour tp ships today. It reads "no non-`PASS` row in the round carries any severity", so a non-`PASS` row whose `severity` is `null` or absent carries no severity and does not keep the round open — that round is clean under `all`. Today the audit record path computes the verdict as `clean := findings == 0` where `findings` counts every non-`PASS` row at any severity, exactly as §1 states one paragraph earlier ("--record counts every row whose status is not exactly PASS, at any severity"). Three statements in this release therefore disagree about the same input: §1 deliverable 1 ("Default `all`, which is the behaviour tp ships today, so a project that does not set it sees no change"), §2's table row, and §7 test 8, which builds `null` and absent fixtures and requires them to fail closed. Measured: the recorded corpus has 360 non-`PASS` rows and none carries a null or absent severity, so the replay in test 10 cannot discriminate the two readings — the only test that could is test 8, and it contradicts the table.
suggestion: State the `all` row without a severity quantifier: `all` — the round has no non-`PASS` row. Keep the severity quantifier only in the `blocking` row. Then §2's following sentence ("Both predicates are over the round's non-PASS rows") is true of both rows, §1's no-change promise holds, and test 8's null/absent fixtures stop contradicting the default.

finding: Test 9 pins no property of its fixture, so even with the observable corrected the named mutation survives on most fixtures an implementer would build. A live re-grade changes the answer only for a round whose non-PASS rows are ALL non-blocking (warning/info only); on a round with zero non-PASS rows, or on one carrying an `error`, `all` and `blocking` agree and the mutation is invisible. Measured on this repository's corpus, 4 of v0.35.0's 9 audit rounds and 3 of v0.36.0's 13 agree under both policies, so a two-round fixture drawn without the rule has a real chance of proving nothing. Secondly, engine.ReviewRoundClean falls back to the stored flag when the round's findings file is missing (internal/engine/reviewclean.go:57-60), so a fixture that synthesises state.json entries without writing audit-round-N.ndjson also survives the mutation.
suggestion: Require the fixture to be self-guarding, in the same way brief_runs_test.go's `require.NotEmpty` guards its divergent fixture: at least one recorded round must carry non-PASS rows of which none is `error` (so its verdict differs between the two policies) and the test must assert that precondition before the comparison; and every recorded round must have a real audit-round-N.ndjson on disk, recorded through `--record`, not a synthesised state entry.

finding: Test 9's observable is the one value the named killing mutation cannot move. It asserts that switching to `blocking` without re-recording "leaves every stored round's verdict unchanged", and names the review twin's live re-grade as the mutation that kills it. Measured against the twin: the review side ALSO stamps at record time -- internal/cli/review_record.go:141 writes `Clean: clean` into state.json and its comment at 189-191 says "the stored ReviewRound.Clean stays the frozen record-time value"; internal/cli/review_status.go:60 says of the live recompute "(this response is not persisted)". So under the live-re-grade design the STORED verdict is byte-identical to the stamped design, and a test written to test 9's own words (record, flip the knob, re-read state.json, compare) passes against its killing mutation. The only observable that separates the two designs is the REPORTED verdict.
suggestion: Reword test 9's observable as the reported verdict on both audit outputs, not the stored one: after recording under `all` and setting `blocking` with no re-record, `tp audit <spec> --status` must emit the same `audit_rounds[].clean` per round, the same `consecutive_clean` and the same `converged` as before the switch, and a `--record` of an unchanged results file must emit the same `clean`. State that reading state.json alone does not discriminate, so the next draft does not re-derive it.

finding: §1 says of `by_severity`: "Emitted unconditionally, so it is the one part every project sees." §6's third reversal contradicts that in the same release. `engine.DivergenceHint` is emitted verbatim as the `hint` field of every divergence object, on both `tp audit --record` and `tp audit --status`, unconditionally and surviving `--compact` — no workflow field gates it. Editing that constant therefore changes agent-visible output for every project that has ever seen a divergence, whatever `audit_converge_on` resolves to, and it changes it on the two commands the loop actually reads, not on `--merge`. So there are two unconditional surfaces in this release, not one, and §1 names the less consequential of the two as the only one.
suggestion: Either withdraw "the one part every project sees" from §1, or promote the `DivergenceHint` edit out of §6's trailing paragraph into §1's deliverable list with the same visibility statement, so an implementer sizing the blast radius from §1 sees both.

finding: "`blocking` governs `clean` and nothing else" is stated as a closed claim and then enumerates only three surfaces (`role_streaks[].open`, `consecutive_clean`, `spec_coverage_clean_rounds`). Two further consumers of the same value are unnamed and behave differently from each other. (a) `next_action` is derived from the round's `clean` on BOTH audit paths — `--record` from the just-computed `clean`, `--status` from the latest stored round's flag — so it does change under `blocking`: it will name the advance-the-phase step while `warning`/`info` rows are open. It is agent-facing, decision-critical and survives `--compact`, and the shipped premise it rests on ("the latest recorded round holding open non-PASS rows is exactly !Clean") is exactly what `blocking` falsifies — a fourth shipped claim reversed, beside §6's three. (b) The round entry's own stored `findings` count stays severity-blind, so a stored round will read `clean: true` beside `findings: 4`. Neither consequence is stated, and both are things an agent reading the payload has to reconcile.
suggestion: Extend §2's enumeration to name every consumer of `clean` and say for each whether it moves: `next_action` (moves, deliberately — say what it should recommend when the round is clean under `blocking` with advisory rows open) and the stored `findings` count (does not move, so `clean: true` beside a non-zero `findings` is expected). Then reconcile §6's "three reversals" with the shipped `next_action` premise.

finding: Round 8's record-time decision leaves "the consuming sink" with no referent I can resolve. If `clean` is stamped at record time and nothing recomputes live, then `tp audit --record` is the ONLY command that ever reads the resolved value — `--status`, `--status --check`, `tp resume` and `tp run` all walk stored `clean` flags through engine.ConsecutiveClean/Converged and never touch the field. So §2's "refused at ... the consuming sink (a validation error)" names one command, while "on the same terms and with the same hint as `review_converge_on`" points at a twin that validates the stored value at review --status AND review --record because both consume it. An implementer has to decide whether `tp audit --status` loads and validates a field it does not use — and the two readings differ in an observable way: under one, a project with a typo in .tp/config.json gets exit 1 from --status; under the other it gets exit 0 and a convergence verdict computed from a config it never checked. §7 test 3's "two exit codes, two commands" counts the write command and one consuming command, so it passes either way.
suggestion: Name the consuming commands explicitly — "`tp audit --record` is the only consuming sink; --status, --check and resume read stored verdicts and do not resolve the field" is a legitimate answer and is one sentence. If --status should validate anyway (parity with the twin, so a bad config is caught before a round is spent), say that instead and make test 3 assert the command by name.

finding: The table that decides the default, and that is the only place an operator is told what the field buys, states its savings under two preconditions it never names, and this release's own new text makes one of them unreachable for the operator it addresses. (1) Set time. §2 decided this round that `clean` is stamped at record time, not recomputed live, and `consecutive_clean` is a trailing run over the stored flags (engine/reviewstate.go:429-438 walks backwards and breaks on the first `!rounds[i].Clean`). So a round recorded before the knob is set keeps `clean: false` forever, and setting `blocking` at round k converges no earlier than k + audit_clean_rounds however advisory rounds 1..k were. §2.1's cells -- `blocking` at round 3 against `all` at round 9 -- are only reachable when the field is set before round 1 is recorded. §2.1 instead closes with `an operator who sets it accepts that trade with the numbers in front of them`, and the numbers that would justify the trade for a given cycle are that cycle's audit rounds, which do not exist yet at the only moment the table's savings are available. §3 hardens this: mid-phase setting is now the expensive path (a fenced write halts the run and spends an operator turn), so the realistic set times are exactly the two the table does not price. (2) `audit_clean_rounds`. Test 10 states that the replay is asserted `at audit_clean_rounds: 2, stated because at 1 the first pair is 2 and 8` -- so the table's four numbers move with a second workflow field. §7 knows both conditions; §2.1, the section a default decision and its documentation are derived from, states neither, and a reader choosing the knob reads §2.1, not the test list.
suggestion: Add both preconditions to §2.1 in one sentence each, next to the table rather than in §7: that the cells assume the field resolved to its value before the cycle's first round was recorded, because §2's record-time stamping means a later set cannot re-grade stored rounds, so a set at round k converges no earlier than k + audit_clean_rounds; and that the cells are computed at audit_clean_rounds: 2. Then say plainly which set time the release supports -- if it is `before the phase opens`, §2.1's closing sentence about numbers in front of the operator should point at the previous cycle's corpus (which exists) rather than this one's (which does not), and the fence's refusal message in §3 should say the same, since it is the one place a unit's operator meets the decision.

finding: Test 11 has no negative control, so an over-broad fence passes it while breaking every unattended write. It asserts only that the three paths exit 2 for `all` and `blocking` and "0 without it" -- i.e. the 0 case is the fence DISABLED, never the fence enabled on a write that does not touch this field. Under TP_UNATTENDED=1, `tp set --workflow audit_clean_rounds=2` and a `tp import` of a task file whose workflow block omits audit_converge_on must both still exit 0; nothing in §7 says so. This is a live risk rather than a hypothetical: the existing hook, fenceWorkflowWrite (internal/cli/unattended.go:56), takes `requested float64` and is dispatched per field, so a string-valued field cannot use it and an implementer must add a new branch -- the cheapest of which fences the command, not the field.
suggestion: Add to test 11 the enabled-fence zero case on all three paths: under TP_UNATTENDED=1, a `tp set --workflow`, a `tp set --workflow --project` and a `tp import` that do not mention audit_converge_on each exit 0 and write what they were asked to write.

finding: The fence is specified on the field, over every write path, with no exemption for a write whose value equals the already-resolved one — and §7 test 11 pins that reading ("exits 2 under `TP_UNATTENDED=1` for both `all` and `blocking`"). `tp import` writes a whole task file, so the fence fires on any import of a task file whose workflow block carries the field, including a re-import of the exact value the operator approved, and including `all`, the built-in default. Under `tp run` that is a stop, not a warning: the unit must file `tp escalate --decision audit-converge-on` for a decision the operator has already made, and the run halts with `stop_reason: escalation` every time it reaches that import. The fence's own justification — "a unit that can set `all` can set `blocking` on the next line" — argues for refusing a *change*, not for refusing the carriage of a value already in force.
suggestion: Say explicitly which of the two the release wants: (a) refuse only a write that differs from the resolved value (and then say how `tp import` computes "the resolved value" for a file it is about to write, and amend test 11), or (b) keep the blanket refusal and state the consequence in §3 — a project that sets this field must keep it in `.tp/config.json`, never in a task file, or no unattended import of that file can ever succeed.

finding: The fence is twice as wide as the argument that justifies it, and the extra half costs the most expensive round-trip tp has. §3 opens by naming the risk exactly -- `the first string-valued workflow field whose non-default value relaxes a gate` -- and then fences both values on this ground: `The fence is on the field, not the direction: a unit that can set `all` can set `blocking` on the next line, so a direction-scoped fence is one a unit walks around.` That argument refutes a fence scoped to the transition (refuse a write that weakens the current value), which a unit can indeed walk around by writing from a state with no stored prior. It does not reach a fence scoped to the literal: refusing any write of `blocking`, from any state, by any path, has no walk-around, because every route to `blocking` is a write of `blocking`. So fencing `all` -- the built-in default, the value the release recommends, and the only value that can tighten the gate rather than relax it -- buys nothing the narrower fence does not already buy. Its price is not a refused command: under `tp run` a fenced write exits 2, the unit records an escalation, the run stops with `stop_reason: escalation`, and a human turn plus a fresh `tp run` is spent -- for a write that cannot end a phase early. §3 routes `tp import` into the same fence, so the halt is reachable from routine decomposition: a task file carrying `audit_converge_on: all` as an explicit override is un-importable under a run, with no lint or validate signal ahead of the import to warn the decomposer. Test 11 pins the cost rather than the value: it asserts exit 2 `for both `all` and `blocking``, doubling the assertions on all three paths.
suggestion: Scope the fence to the value that relaxes the gate: every write path refuses `blocking` under TP_UNATTENDED=1 and lets `all` through, and replace the direction argument with the reason it actually supports -- a value-scoped fence has no walk-around because every route to `blocking` writes `blocking`. Halve test 11 accordingly and add one assertion that a unit may write `all` under TP_UNATTENDED=1 (the killing mutation is a fence keyed on the field name). If refusing `all` is deliberate -- for instance because no unit may touch convergence policy at all, in either direction -- state that as the rationale and price it: name that an import of a task file carrying `audit_converge_on: all` halts a run, and say what warns the decomposer before the import unit runs.

finding: §3 newly extends the fence to tp import — "Every path that writes the field under TP_UNATTENDED=1 exits 2 — including tp import" — and test 11 pins it for both all and blocking. tp import does not reach fenceWorkflowWrite at all; it assigns the whole workflow block (importcmd.go:158-162 via importedHasWorkflowKey), and when the imported document carries NO workflow key it copies the EXISTING file's block forward: tf.Workflow = existing.Workflow. So once a project has ever set audit_converge_on, every later import re-writes it, and a fence on "writes the field" refuses every subsequent import. Under tp run that is CLAUDE.md Workflow A step 6, so the release's own opt-in users would deadlock their decompose→import step on a value that changes nothing. The spec never distinguishes setting the field from carrying it forward, and nothing in the round-7 snapshot required tp import to be fenced at all — its fence sentence closed over tp set --workflow and its --project form.
suggestion: State the boundary the fence is over: a write that CHANGES the resolved value, or an explicit occurrence of the key in the imported document (importedHasWorkflowKey already computes exactly that), not a preserved carry-forward. Test 11 should pin the preserving import as exit 0, otherwise the release ships a deadlock for the projects that opt in.

finding: §3's two normative sentences give opposite answers on a third input that `tp import` really produces, and test 11 tests only two. "Every path that WRITES the field" reads as: fence when the incoming document mentions audit_converge_on. "The fence is on the field, not the direction" reads as: fence whenever the effective value moves. They diverge on a REMOVAL. Measured in internal/cli/importcmd.go:154-162, workflow preservation applies only when the imported document carries no top-level `workflow` key; a `{...}` import whose workflow block is present but omits audit_converge_on therefore REPLACES a target's stored `blocking` with nothing, changing the resolved value to the built-in `all` -- a write of the field by the second reading and not by the first. Test 11 pins "for both `all` and `blocking`", so both implementations pass it and they disagree on real input.
suggestion: Decide the removal case in §3 in one sentence -- e.g. "a write that removes the key from a layer that carried it is a write of the field and is refused on the same terms" -- and add it to test 11 as a third input on the tp import path, with the fixture being an existing task file carrying audit_converge_on=blocking and an imported document whose workflow block omits it.

finding: §4 pins two of by_severity's four input cases and leaves the key type undecidable for the other two. "A row with an unrecognised severity is counted under the literal it carries, and one with none under `null`" — but by_severity is a JSON object, so `null` cannot be a key; it has to be the STRING "null", or the string "", or an omitted bucket, and the three are different payloads for the agent that parses them. Two further cases have no answer at all: a row whose `severity` key is absent (distinct from present-and-null, and §7 test 8 makes that distinction load-bearing for the predicate), and a row whose severity is a non-string JSON value. The twin loop shows what happens by default: audit_merge.go:65 does `status, _ := r["status"].(string)`, so a non-string lands in the empty-string bucket silently. §4's own justification — "the breakdown never hides a row the predicate would block on" — is exactly what these three cases decide, and test 13 ("correct over a mixed round") pins no key name, so an implementation bucketing all three under "" passes it.
suggestion: Name the keys. E.g.: an unrecognised string severity is its own key; a `severity` that is JSON null, absent, or not a string is counted under the single key "unrecognized" (or three named keys, if they should stay distinct). Then have test 13 assert the key names, not just presence — a breakdown whose bucket names are unspecified cannot be read by the agent it is emitted for.

finding: §4's keying rule for by_severity is undefined over two of the four row shapes the release must handle, so test 13's "correct" cannot be written deterministically. (a) "one with none under `null`": a JSON object key is a string, so this is `{"null": 1}`, `{"": 1}`, or a key omitted entirely -- three incompatible readings, and the count is decision-relevant because §4 says the breakdown "never hides a row the predicate would block on". (b) "a row with an unrecognised severity is counted under the literal it carries" is undefined when the literal is not a string: nothing rejects `"severity": 3` or `"severity": true` on the audit path (audit_record.go validates `category` only), and Go's `row["severity"].(string)` collapses a number, a bool and an absent key to the same empty string -- so the natural implementation silently merges cases (a) and (b), which is precisely the hiding §4 forbids. Measured: every severity in all 360 recorded non-PASS rows is a string, so the corpus supplies no instance and this will first appear in the field.
suggestion: State the key for each shape as a literal: absent or JSON `null` -> key `"null"`; a non-empty string -> that string verbatim; any other JSON type -> its compact JSON encoding (`"3"`, `"true"`) rather than being folded into the null bucket. Add the non-string row to test 13's fixture and to test 8's fail-closed fixtures, which today enumerate three shapes and imply completeness.

finding: Reported as a RECURRENCE, not a new class: round 7 raised `scope-in-a-non-goal` against the old §4, the cut moved the text, and the shape survived it. §1 opens "**Three deliverables**" and enumerates §2, §3, §4. §6 is titled "Non-Goals" — a section whose contract is what the release does not do — and its closing bolded paragraph then states required work: three shipped assertions must be reversed, `SKILL.md` must change, and `engine.DivergenceHint` (a shipped constant in agent-facing output) must be rewritten. §7 test 14 tests it, so it is a deliverable with a test and no owning section. Decomposition reads §1 for the task list; an implementer who takes §1 at its word ships three deliverables and a red gate.
suggestion: Move the reversal paragraph out of §6 into a numbered §1 deliverable (4. The reversals, §x) with its own short section, and leave §6 holding only things the release does not do. The mechanical test: every paragraph in a Non-Goals section should be deletable without changing what gets built.

finding: The rewrite renumbered the sections and reordered the Non-Goals, and three live pointers in spec/0.46.0.md now resolve to the wrong text. (1) 0.46.0.md:334 — "The breakdown on tp audit --merge is not deferred: spec/0.37.0.md Non-Goal 6 takes it". Non-Goal 6 is now "A fourth row status"; the breakdown moved to §4 and Non-Goal 4. (2) 0.46.0.md:332 — "An earlier draft of this paragraph said tp emits no count at all; that was false and spec/0.37.0.md §2 said so on the same day". The correction now lives in §4; the current §2 does not say it. (3) 0.46.0.md:384 — "the sentence is here because it was written in spec/0.37.0.md §3 and lost in the cut". §3 is now "The fence"; the cut is §5. All three break silently, because each still resolves to a real section.
suggestion: Either restore the numbering the sibling spec points at, or correct the three pointers in spec/0.46.0.md (§8.3 twice, §8.4 once) in the same change. Since spec/0.46.0.md is unshipped, editing it is permitted; leaving it is not, because a pointer that resolves to the wrong section is worse than a dangling one.

finding: The third reversal names two artifacts and the release has to move three. §6 says the reversals are the gate guard's assertion, "the docs-contract guard pinning a `SKILL.md` sentence", and `engine.DivergenceHint`. But the guard that ties the constant to a document reads `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md`, not `SKILL.md`: REFERENCE.md quotes `engine.DivergenceHint` verbatim (measured — the full 4-clause constant string is present in REFERENCE.md and absent from SKILL.md), and the docs-contract guard asserts REFERENCE.md contains the shipped constant precisely so the two cannot drift. SKILL.md carries its own separate sentence ending "still counts every non-PASS row". So changing the constant makes the gate red until REFERENCE.md is edited byte-for-byte with it — a required edit no section of this release names, and §7 test 14 ("asserted against the shipped docs-contract guard, so the documentation cannot drift from the constant") describes that guard while naming the wrong document.
suggestion: Name all three artifacts that move together in §6 — `engine.DivergenceHint`, its verbatim copy in `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md`, and the independent `SKILL.md` sentence — and make test 14 assert the constant against REFERENCE.md (the guard that actually holds them together) and SKILL.md separately.

finding: No test guards Non-Goal 2 against the predicate this release adds, and the failure mode is the same "natural thing to copy" that test 9 exists to block. `tp audit --resolve` ships today (internal/cli/audit_resolve.go) and writes a `resolved` object onto a row; the record path deliberately ignores it -- countAuditFindings (audit_record.go:248) counts every non-PASS row regardless. The model an implementer will reach for when writing the audit severity predicate is engine.ReviewRoundClean, whose surviving set is computed by reviewFindingResolvedAway (reviewclean.go:32-43,64-66). Copying that helper along with the severity test ships Non-Goal 2 -- a disposition that stops blocking -- while every test in §7 stays green, because tests 5-8 use rows that carry no `resolved` key at all.
suggestion: Add a test: a round whose only non-PASS row is `error` carrying `resolved: {status: "wontfix", evidence: "..."}` is NOT clean under either value of audit_converge_on, and the round's recorded `findings` count still includes it. Name the killing mutation as folding reviewFindingResolvedAway (or rowDisposed) into the audit clean predicate.

finding: Test 13 is the only test in the list that names neither an input nor a mutation, against §7's own opening rule that "Each test names the input that makes it fail" -- tests 5/6/7 name a severity, 8 names three fixtures, 9 names the live re-grade, 10 names the re-recording. "Correct over a mixed round" leaves the fixture entirely open, and one omission is load-bearing: §4 restricts by_severity to non-`PASS` rows, and a fixture of only non-PASS rows cannot test that restriction. Measured, an implementation counting every row would bucket PASS rows under the no-severity key, because all 2,913 PASS rows in v0.35.0+v0.36.0 carry `severity: null` -- so the restriction is only observable when the fixture carries PASS rows too. Two engineers write different fixtures and only one of them can fail.
suggestion: Pin test 13's fixture and its killing mutation: a round carrying at least one PASS row (whose severity must NOT appear in by_severity), one `error`, one `warning`, one `info`, one row with a severity outside the enum and one with none; assert the exact map, not just presence. Name the two mutations: counting all rows rather than non-PASS rows, and moving the assignment inside `--merge`'s existing `if !IsCompact()` block (internal/cli/audit_merge.go:90).

finding: Test 14 says "The two surviving assertions of the gate guard still pass". The round-7 snapshot said nine, and nine is the measured number: internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go:469-503 carries eleven assert/require calls (:473, :474, :481, :484, :485, :490, :493, :494, :497, :498, :500) and the reversal is :473-:474 only, so 9 survive. The rewrite also contradicts its own §6, which says "Every other assertion in those guards stands". finding: The table's two convergence columns are meaningless without `audit_clean_rounds`, and §2.1 never names it. I re-derived every cell from `spec/.tp-review/*/audit-round-*.ndjson`: at `audit_clean_rounds: 2` the table is exact (v0.35.0 `blocking` 3 / `all` 9; v0.36.0 `blocking` 3 / `all` never), and at 1 the first row becomes 2 and 8 — a different table. Second, smaller: the v0.36.0 row's `blocking` cell is a counterfactual — under `blocking` that cycle halts at round 3 and rounds 7, 12 and 13 are never recorded, so the `error` rows the prose relies on exist only because the loop kept running under `all`. finding: The fence as specified has no exemption for a write that changes nothing, and `tp import` is where that bites. §3 fences "every path that writes the field" on the field rather than the direction, and §7 test 11 requires `tp import` to exit 2 under TP_UNATTENDED=1 "for both `all` and `blocking`". But import does not set a value — it writes a whole task file, workflow block included (engine.LoadTaskWorkflowOverride reads that block and §2 makes the task layer a legal home for the field). So a project that has committed `audit_converge_on` in its <base>.tasks.json can never run `tp import` under `tp run`: the decompose→import unit exits 2 on a file whose value the operator himself committed and which the run would resolve to identically either way. The cap fields avoid this precisely by comparing against the resolved value (engine.UnattendedRaise, and cli/unattended.go's refuseUnattendedRaise), and §3's argument against a direction-scoped fence — "a unit that can set `all` can set `blocking` on the next line" — is an argument about `tp set`, not about a bulk import of an unchanged file.
suggestion: Say what import does with a value that already resolves. Either exempt a write whose resulting resolved value is unchanged (the fence still stops a unit introducing or flipping the field, which is the failure §3 names), or state that a project adopting this field cannot import unattended and must escalate — and then say so where an operator will read it before adopting the field, not only in the fence section.

finding: The snapshot carried a measured negative result about the fence mechanism and the rewrite dropped it with the survey: fenceWorkflowWrite has signature (field string, requested float64) — numeric by signature — and all four call sites (set.go:414, set.go:428, set_project.go:98, set_project.go:108) sit after ParseFloat/Atoi, so a string field reaches none of them. Still true in the tree today. The snapshot's conclusion was that "widening the numeric fence" ships a SILENT no-op and that the string-shaped fence to copy is the FencedCommandField guard placed before the type dispatch. §3 now says only "Every path that writes the field under TP_UNATTENDED=1 exits 2", which is the decision — but the natural implementation of that decision is the one measured not to work, and test 11 (exit 2 per path) would redden rather than pass, costing a cycle to rediscover. This is not a citation a later round re-falsifies; it is a negative result, and negative results are what CLAUDE.md's "prove a fix by running it" rule exists to preserve.
suggestion: Keep one sentence: the fence is not a widening of the numeric cap fence, which a string value never reaches. It is a decision about mechanism selection, not a survey of line numbers, and it survives without any citation.

finding: §3's escalation paragraph kept the decision (add audit-converge-on to the --decision enum) but dropped the boundary that came with it. The enum is closed over five values (engine/escalation.go:21-27, with the comment at :19 reading "not a sixth category") and its cardinality is asserted in several places that must move together; more importantly, the snapshot recorded that spec/0.35.0.md:428-429 closes the set over five, is a SHIPPED spec, and is therefore "recorded as superseded rather than edited" — citing spec/0.34.0.md Non-Goal 6, which forbids editing a shipped spec. A unit told to "add audit-converge-on to that enum" and finding a shipped spec that closes the set over five has no instruction not to edit it.
suggestion: Add a clause to §3 or a seventh Non-Goal: the enum grows to six and every shipped spec that closes it over five is recorded as superseded, not edited. The count of assertion sites can go to task acceptance; the don't-edit-a-shipped-spec boundary cannot.

finding: §4 cites `nonblocking_open` as the precedent -- `It is emitted unconditionally and survives --compact, on the same grounds the review side gives for nonblocking_open` -- and takes half of it. The twin is conditional, and the shipped comment says so in the same breath as the --compact grounds this release is borrowing: review_status.go:130-134, `Emitted solely when that round is clean and the count is positive, so the field's mere presence signals the accepted-open state; absent on a non-clean latest round, on a clean one with zero non-blocking survivors, and under review_converge_on=all` (review_record.go:224-231 is the same). The conditionality is not incidental to the --compact argument, it is what makes it true: the field survives --compact because its presence is itself the decision, and a key emitted on every payload signals nothing by being there. Dropping that half has three costs. (a) The signal is gone: an agent must read the map's contents to learn what the presence of the key would have told it. (b) It lands on every `tp audit --merge` of every project, and the default is `all` (§2), which is the one case the twin excludes by name -- under `all` any non-PASS row blocks, so the breakdown changes no convergence decision there, and it is derivable from the merged rows that same command emits. (c) §1 then advertises that as the benefit: `Emitted unconditionally, so it is the one part every project sees` -- the sentence sells the cost half of the trade as the value.
suggestion: Keep --compact survival (the grounds hold) and restore the conditionality the precedent supplies: emit `by_severity` only when the round has at least one non-`PASS` row, so absence means nothing was graded away and presence beside `clean: true` is the discounted-round signal, exactly as `nonblocking_open` behaves. Reword §1's third deliverable from `Emitted unconditionally, so it is the one part every project sees` to what it then is -- the breakdown a project sees when a round had non-`PASS` rows. Test 13 already asserts presence over a mixed round and survival under --compact; add the arm the change needs, a clean-under-`all` round with no non-`PASS` rows where the key is absent (the killing mutation is unconditional emission of an empty map).

finding: Test 14's title claims a quantifier the test it describes cannot check. "The three reversals and nothing more" is an exhaustiveness claim over every assertion in the suite, while the described procedure checks two named assertions in one guard plus two documentation strings. Nothing in it could fail on a fourth reversal elsewhere, and the procedure a reader would substitute -- run the suite, see it green -- is a tautology: a reversed assertion is one that was rewritten to pass, so a green suite after the change is evidence of nothing about how many were changed. This is the repository's own "never assert a quantifier you did not count" rule applied to a test rather than to prose, and it is the one test whose failure would tell a reader that the release touched more than it claimed.
suggestion: Either drop "and nothing more" and let test 14 assert only what it checks, or bind the quantifier to an artifact that can drift-check itself -- e.g. commit the three reversed assertions as a named list and have the task's acceptance derive the diff of changed assertions from `git diff` against that list, in task acceptance where it is checked by running, per this file's own rewrite banner.

finding: Two near-misses caught before they were written.
